description: We’re a small team building a game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players will plan a space mission by choosing a destination, spacecraft, payload and budget, then see the consequences. We’re comfortable with coding and web development and want to make it fun, not just educational. We’re looking for someone who can handle graphic design, animation or storytelling to help with art, UI and mission scenarios.
summary:
The Mission Architect is a web-based software application, where you have to assume the role of the mission designer of NASA. Selecting the scientific objective, selecting the instrument, designing the spacecraft, selecting the orbit and the launch vehicle – flying the mission – these are your responsibilities. However, your decisions will have an engineering effect; the array which was optimal for the Earth mission doesn't work on Mars, and there is more data from the instrument than you can transmit to Earth. Four users can assume the role of the mission designer in the Mission Architect, but they control their subsystems only. The main idea of the application is as follows: real missions do not use all of the money in their budget. They leave a margin of 10-35 percent.
They are launched into the simulation, and the tests of these design models will compare them to actual recorded coronal mass ejections in the DONKI archive database of NASA. This is followed by listing all 10,368 designs in order to form the efficient frontier. Plot the surface to scale, outpost your array, battery and links that you have purchased in preparation for the body you will launch into orbit, land 20 units of your hardware, but you still need an orbiter to relay your data. All numbers come from NASA documentation.
details:
The Mission Architect is an interactive mission design and verification system. You set up your science objective, choose the instruments, design your spacecraft bus, select your orbit and launch vehicle, and you get to fly the outcome. One engine does all of the calculations from your selections, and each error shows you the figures and what to do to fix it: "Array produces 1620 W orbit-average at end of life; spacecraft uses 1652 W (-2% margin)."

Three ideas carry the project.

1. Margin is the mechanic

Real-life missions never use 100% of their budget. A margin of 10 to 35 percent of the budget is held back as an additional fund since all estimates go up in development as instrumentation becomes heavier, software uses more processor times, and delays increase costs. Here the margin is the real number, but not the one hidden inside.

The margin includes all margins: all margins having values less than zero in weight, power, and budget will make your mission fail. All margins within 0 to 10 percent range are considered as risky and at your first problem during flight, it will mean your failure. All margins between 10 to 35 percent are classified as nominal margins and earn a bonus of ten points. Margins more than 50 percent are called as overdesign, and will be punished due to costs of extra margins and extra Watts of power have to be supplied by solar cells.

2. Flown against real NASA data, not just checked

Design is not an option but a task. Flight Console takes the craft along its actual orbit, entering the eclipse, maneuvering behind the planet and linking to the ground station during the contact period. Strip chart provides recording of the array power, state of charge of the battery and fill of recorder as a function of time. Scrubber starts at the launch of the craft and flies along the same orbit as an array of the designated age.

Series is simply a representation in time domain of the values already available from the engine and test set will ensure that exactly that is done. It calculates numbers that are impossible to calculate using static design approach – the design of Mars mission on an S band link will fill its recorder in 2.3 days and lose 56.3 GigaBytes of data daily.

Design validation will be done through actual CME data from the DONKI database of NASA with velocities and the satellites that have recorded them. There are three cases under which the mission will come to an end as a result of the storm, namely inadequacy of power margin, inadequacy of data margin, or one point failure of the attitude control system without any redundancies. The choice of orbit influences the exposure factor by a factor of five, which is reasonable in view of the fact that the magnetosphere of the earth shields LEO but not those that approach the moon and those that approach Mars. DONKI offers CORS headers and so, there is a static access to it without any backend processing. In case of API errors, the same data snap is used.

3. Not one design, every design.

The execution of the engine takes 0.013 ms, providing a unique opportunity to enumerate all the space rather than sample it. All 10,368 possible permutations of spacecraft buses are calculated in the browser within 100 ms and presented as a trade-off between science and cost, wherein the efficient frontier is drawn through them and your own solution is marked on it. Out of 10,368 combinations, 76 are feasible for the default goal: 0.7%. In case of a Mars mission with a score of 41, the system shows dominating solutions and diffs for each part with one click.

What your design builds on the ground

The orbiter represents just the first phase of the mission, but not all the elements of the mission. In this case, the surface segment will use your array, battery, link, launcher, and equipment, and will build, according to the scale relative to 1.8 m crew, all the structures that were purchased: solar farm, pressurized hab modules, battery modules, ground station, radiators, volatile processing unit, landing pads, and radiation shelter. The day/night cycle is regulated through the shadow of the Sun, and the orbiter that you design flies over and provides the relay link.

No single part of this drawing is unnecessary. All the structural elements have sizes based upon a number reported by the engine previously, a table underneath gives the calculations for each of the headline numbers, and the eleven numbers that the mission physics do not provide are declared assumptions, rather than buried within an art asset. It delivers the toughest lesson in the entire exercise: you can deploy twenty copies of your instrument suite, but you still need that orbiter to retrieve the data.

Four people, four roles, one spacecraft

Mission design is an argument between specialists, so up to four people can take part. One player creates a session and reads out a five-character code, and each player then takes a single role. The Mission Planner decides the objective, the orbit and the launch vehicle. Science decides which instruments fly. Engineering decides the bus that has to carry them. Operations decides the mission lifetime and when to fly it. You see the screens you control and the margins everyone shares, and any change to a field you do not own is refused. Nobody can overrule anybody, and that limitation is what forces the discussion.

Learning by failing, then getting to know why

The levels of difficulty will set the amount of explanation that will be given by the game, as well as the level of reserve; however, the physics will stay the same: Cadet will give explanations to all screens and cushion events; Flight Director will turn off all hints and will preserve the design of the game on the same level as in the original software. As a result of debriefing, you will find out the source of your score term by term, starting with the smallest margin; what will be left after the deal, taking into account the trade study; what storm of reality will get you down; and which of your actions will be the most effective considering your position. There is a game assistant called ArchitectX, who will provide the answers to your mission via the same engine that the screens use; thus, there is no need for an API key, and the assistant works offline and does not make up figures.

Tools and engineering

React 19, Vite 8, CSS only, and PeerJS for collaboration among the team members. A static site without a server, without a database, and without user accounts. Three fonts using open licenses and self-hosted, so that no third-party code is loaded at runtime. All numbers are owned by one engine, and no screen does any calculation of its own; hence, the simulation, storm validation, trading analysis, and the surface component can never clash with each other. There are eight test suites that control all changes, and these test suites are run by CI on every push to GitHub, and the website cannot be deployed until all eight pass. The physics is standard and well known; inverse-square solar flux of 1361 W/m2, array degradation depending on radiation index, Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for propellant, link budget depending on the power of transmission and antenna aperture, and cost model with integration factor of 1.35x.

Intended impact

They analyze each one separately without understanding their interrelation. The budget for power varies according to the change in orbit. An additional instrument added in the spacecraft leads to failure in downlink. Give no margin whatsoever and an ordinary coronal mass ejection will end the mission. This is a fact which cannot be gained through any book but a simulator provides the interaction in just seconds whenever one likes. The simulator was created for classroom training purposes either in high school or for freshmen students in college where four students could undertake four different roles.

AI Assistance

Two things kept separate. Within the product itself, ArchitectX is a keyword assistant, not a language model: no API key, no inference, no internet access, and identified as such wherever it comes up for users. In the process of building it, we used Claude (Anthropic) as our code assistant: helping generate and review module implementations, writing test suites, and reviewing physics and copy. Engineering decisions, constants, NASA sources, and calibration targets were selected and validated by the team, and the engine is tested against eight test suites which must pass before anything gets published. Our use of AI is allowable under submission guidelines and we disclose it.
